design_detail: Within-person, placebo-controlled human laboratory study in a full-motion driving simulator (National Advanced Driving Simulator, University of Iowa). Six sessions at least 1 week apart, in randomized order: placebo, low-THC (2.9%) or high-THC (6.7%) vaporized cannabis (500 mg, inhaled ad libitum over 10 minutes), each with an oral placebo or alcohol drink aimed at an approximate peak breath alcohol of 0.065%. Each person drove a 45-minute night route 0.5 to 1.3 hours after the start of cannabis dosing. Blood THC and breath alcohol during the drive were modelled from samples taken before and after it, and lateral-control measures were analysed by event against those modelled concentrations (stepwise general linear model, SAS GLM Select, Schwarz information criterion) rather than by dose condition. 19 people drove; 18 were analysed. A registry number is cited (NCT01620177); the record was not read. Double-blinding is stated only in the Discussion and Conclusion.
can_establish: In 18 healthy people who used cannabis occasionally, in a simulator and in the conditions given, that blood THC and breath alcohol during the drive were each associated with more lane weave (SDLP), that alcohol but not THC was associated with more lane departures and lateral acceleration, and roughly how much lane weave a given blood THC level gave compared with a given breath alcohol level.
cannot_establish: Real-road driving or crash risk (the authors say SDLP is not directly validated against crashes; one simulator, one 45-minute night drive per condition); whether cannabis with alcohol is worse than the sum of the two (the stepwise model selected no interaction term, but the study gives no estimate or interval for it, and its by-condition tests were not significant for either drug); effects at alcohol levels above the target of about 0.065% (the range of during-drive concentrations analysed is not reported); effects in regular cannabis smokers, in women (5 of 18), at other ages, or with other drugs or sleep loss.

sample.recruitment: Not described. The paper says only that healthy adults gave written consent in an Institutional Review Board-approved study run with the University of Iowa Clinical Research Unit and the driving simulator (Methods › 2.1; Acknowledgments). Participants entered the clinical research unit 10 to 16 hours before drug administration, to rule out acute intoxication.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 21 to 55; cannabis use at least once in 3 months but no more than 3 days a week over the past 3 months (Cannabis Use Disorders Identification Test); light or moderate alcohol use on the Quantity-Frequency-Variability scale or, if heavy, no more than 3 to 4 servings on a typical occasion; licensed driver for at least 2 years; at least 1,300 miles driven in the past year. Excluded: clinically significant illness; a clinically significant adverse event with cannabis or alcohol, or motion sickness; blood donation in the past 2 weeks; pregnancy or nursing; interest in drug treatment in the past 60 days; medicines contraindicated with cannabis or alcohol or known to affect driving; need for non-standard driving equipment; earlier participation in a similar simulator study (Methods › 2.1).
sample.demographics: 19 entered: 13 men and 6 women, ages 21 to 37 (mean 26.1, SD 4.1), 74% White, mean body mass index 26.3. Most used cannabis at least twice a month and up to 3 days a week; last use a median of 4 days before admission (range 0.3 to 120 days); 6 to 23 years of driving (median 10). The 18 analysed: 13 men and 5 women (editors' count from Table 1), mean age 26.3 (SD 4.2).
sample.attrition: No dropouts reported. Participant 12 (a woman) was excluded from all driving analyses because her data were extreme in almost every measure and condition, including placebo with placebo, and videos showed erratic, inattentive driving in all conditions. No rule set in advance and no analysis that keeps her data are reported.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers who passed medical screening, had no serious past reaction to cannabis or alcohol, were willing to drink and inhale before driving, and were experienced drivers; only occasional cannabis smokers and light-to-moderate drinkers aged 21 to 37. The authors note that participants knew their driving was observed and might have driven more carefully, or wanted to show that cannabis does not affect driving.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered. Alcohol: 90% grain alcohol in fruit juice drunk ad libitum over 10 minutes, or placebo juice with an alcohol-swabbed rim and 1 mL alcohol on top to mimic taste and smell. Cannabis: 500 mg of vaporized cannabis supplied by NIDA (Volcano Medic vaporizer) inhaled ad libitum over 10 minutes: placebo 0.008%, low 2.9% or high 6.7% THC. Blood THC assayed by a published method (protein precipitation, solid-phase extraction; linear range 1 to 100 µg/L) at 0.17, 0.42, 1.4 and 2.3 hours after inhalation, oral fluid collected alongside; breath alcohol (Alco-Sensor IV) at the same times. Concentrations during the drive were modelled: individual power-curve regression for THC, linear interpolation for alcohol.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: placebo, low or high vaporized cannabis (500 mg containing 0.008%, 2.9% or 6.7% THC) inhaled over 10 minutes, after a placebo or alcohol drink drunk over 10 minutes (target peak breath alcohol about 0.065%); six single-dose sessions at least 1 week apart; the drive began 0.5 to 1.3 hours after the start of cannabis dosing. Because inhalation was ad libitum, achieved THC overlapped between the two active doses: 6 of 18 people had a higher peak blood THC after the low dose than after the high dose, and 4 had peaks within 20% of each other despite a two-fold dose difference (Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Figure 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were occasional cannabis smokers and light-to-moderate alcohol drinkers; people taking medicines known to affect driving were excluded; no urine or other drug screen is mentioned. Blood THC at the pre-dose baseline sample was above zero in some sessions (maximum 6.3 µg/L, Table 6), which shows residual THC or use between sessions. Not otherwise controlled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants entered the unit 10 to 16 hours before dosing to rule out acute intoxication; last cannabis use before admission a median of 4 days earlier (range 0.3 to 120 days; Table 1). Abstinence was not verified beyond the baseline blood sample.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant drove under all six conditions, including placebo cannabis with placebo alcohol. The Discussion and Conclusion call the design double-blind and placebo-controlled; the Methods describe no blinding procedure beyond the placebo preparations.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person). Condition order was randomized (method not described). Three drive scenarios with varied event order were used across the six drives to limit practice effects; how scenarios were assigned to conditions is not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Stable between-person differences are absorbed by the subject term (the drug-free predicted SDLP ranged from 24.7 to 44.8 cm across people, a spread larger than the drug effects). Not measured or not reported: sleep and time of day before each session, caffeine or tobacco, tolerance beyond self-reported use, expectancy about the drugs, and learning across the six drives.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants as the active conditions.

outcomes.instruments: NADS-1 simulator (a 1996 sedan in a 7.3 m dome with full motion). One 45-minute night drive with urban (25 to 45 mph), interstate (70 mph) and rural segments, other traffic and hazards. Measures: standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP, cm), standard deviation of steering-wheel angle (curvy and straight events), lane departures per minute, maximum lateral acceleration (events with and without sharp turns). Each was analysed by event with speed limit and curvature as covariates. Blood and oral fluid THC and breath alcohol were measured to model exposure.
outcomes.validity_norms: SDLP is described by the authors as a sensitive and widely used measure in drug-driving research but not directly validated against crash risk (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). They take about 2.4 cm, the SDLP increase linked to a blood alcohol of 0.05 in a report they cite (Lococo and Staplin, 2006; not read), as the lowest criterion of impairment. No norms for the simulator are given.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment is an increase in a lateral-control measure relative to the drug-free drive, expressed in centimetres and as a percentage of the drug-free median (31.4 cm at 55 mph on a straight road). The paper sets no threshold for unsafe driving; the equivalences between THC and alcohol levels are read from the model's point estimates.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Terms entered each of the six models (Table 2) by the Bayesian information criterion; there was no adjustment across models, and hundreds of other performance variables were monitored in the study but are not reported here.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes are automated simulator records. The exclusion of participant 12 followed review of the data and driving videos; whether the reviewers knew the condition is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: SDLP model (18 drivers; error df 1,916; model F 28.24): blood THC b = 0.26 cm per µg/L (SE 0.07, t = 3.6, p = 0.0004); breath alcohol b = 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L (SE 0.15, t = 2.9, p = 0.0037); no THC by alcohol term and no quadratic terms selected; speed limit 0.50 (SE 0.03) and inverse curvature 464 (SE 49) significant. Editors' calculation, estimate ± 1.96 SE (normal approximation): THC 0.12 to 0.40 cm per µg/L; alcohol 0.13 to 0.71 cm per 0.01 g/210 L; probably too narrow, because many events within each drive are treated as independent (reporting issue 6). Model predictions at 55 mph on a straight road against a drug-free median of 31.4 cm (between-person range 24.7 to 44.8): THC 5, 10 and 20 µg/L: +1.3, +2.6 and +5.2 cm (4.1%, 8.2%, 16%); breath alcohol 0.05, 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L: +2.1, +3.4 and +4.2 cm (6.7%, 11%, 13%); THC 5 µg/L with 0.05 g/210 L: +3.4 cm (11%), the same as 0.08 g/210 L alone, because the additive model sums the two effects (Table 3). The paper states that about 8.2 and 13.1 µg/L THC gave lane weave like 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L, without intervals. Editors' calculation (delta method on the two slopes, covariance ignored): the THC level matching 0.05 g/210 L is about 8 µg/L with an approximate 95% interval of about 1 to 15 µg/L. Lane departures per minute: alcohol b = 0.030 (SE 0.009, p = 0.0055); maximum lateral acceleration, non-sharp events: alcohol b = 0.0023 m/s² (SE 0.0007, p = 0.0005); THC not selected in either; steering-angle variability and sharp-event acceleration: neither drug. By administered condition (Table 5; no tests or intervals), mean SDLP against 28.8 cm for placebo with placebo: alcohol alone 32.3 cm (+12%); low THC alone 31.3 (+9%); high THC alone 31.2 (+8%); low THC with alcohol 34.2 (+19%); high THC with alcohol 32.2 (+12%). Repeated-measures linear mixed model by achieved peak THC group (Table 4), SDLP: THC group p = 0.28, alcohol p = 0.067, THC by alcohol p = 0.24; the authors call it low-powered.
analysis.covariates: Speed limit, inverse road curvature and a subject term (17 df) in the SDLP model; sex, age, driving experience, usual cannabis and alcohol use, and drive scenario were not entered.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A ClinicalTrials.gov number is given (NCT01620177, Effects of Inhaled Cannabis on Driving Performance). The record was not read, so its registration date, registered outcomes and analysis plan were not compared with the paper. The paper describes its model-selection procedure as aimed at describing the data without assuming which terms would matter.
analysis.selective_reporting: Hundreds of performance variables were monitored; only the lateral-control subset is reported, as the first of a series of papers. The by-condition mixed models (Table 4) were not significant and are set aside as low-powered in favour of the concentration-based model; one participant was excluded after the data were reviewed, with no analysis that keeps her; no correction across six models.
analysis.power: No sample-size or power calculation is reported; 18 people analysed. The authors suggest that a simulator study with 80 participants (Downey et al., 2013) detected cannabis effects on lane straddling that this study did not because of higher power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 18 healthy occasional cannabis smokers in a simulator, modelled blood THC and breath alcohol during the drive were each associated with greater lane weave (0.26 cm per µg/L; 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L). Lane departures and lateral acceleration rose with alcohol but not THC. The stepwise model selected no THC by alcohol term, so its combined predictions are sums. Descriptive means by administered condition do not order by THC dose (low and high THC alone +9% and +8%; with alcohol +19% and +12%), and the by-group mixed model found no significant THC, alcohol or interaction effect on SDLP.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state that cannabis and alcohol effects on SDLP were “additive rather than synergistic”, and that during-drive blood THC of 8.2 and 13.1 µg/L increased SDLP like breath alcohol of 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L, with THC at or above 8.2 µg/L described as matching notably impairing alcohol levels. The Discussion calls the design rigorous, says the observed increase may be substantial enough to count as impairment, says simulator use is not a significant limitation, and recalls that cannabis roughly doubled crash risk in two meta-analyses (Discussion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; 4.1, 5th paragraph). The Discussion also calls the models descriptive; the abstract does not.

timeline.event: Robbe (Hum Psychopharmacol), an on-road study whose title reports cannabis impairment as moderate alone and severe with alcohol (cited by Hartman et al.; not read).

Ramaekers, Robbe and O’Hanlon (Hum Psychopharmacol), on-road: as summarised by Hartman et al., THC at 100 to 300 µg/kg raised SDLP by 1.7 to 3.5 cm, THC at 100 or 200 µg/kg with a target blood alcohol of 0.04% raised it by 5.3 and 8.5 cm, and only the combinations significantly raised time out of lane (not read).
Lenné et al. (Accid Anal Prev), simulator: independent effects of cannabis and alcohol and no interaction, like this study (as described by Hartman et al.; not read).

Ronen et al. (Accid Anal Prev), simulator: lane-position variability rose significantly only when 13 mg THC and alcohol at 0.05% were combined, although neither drug alone had a significant effect (as described by Hartman et al.; not read).

Li et al. (Epidemiol Rev) and Asbridge et al. (BMJ), two meta-analyses of crash studies that Hartman et al. describe as showing about doubled crash risk with cannabis; the second is read for this library.

Downey et al. (Accid Anal Prev), simulator, 80 participants: dose-dependent cannabis effects on straddling lane barrier or solid lines, with or without alcohol (as described by Hartman et al.; not read).
Two companion papers from the same sessions report oral fluid and blood cannabinoid kinetics (Hartman et al., 2015a and 2015b; not read; not independent of this study).

Dubois et al. (Forensic Sci Int), 150,010 US drivers blood-tested after fatal crashes (1991 to 2008): the odds of a police-recorded unsafe driver action with THC and alcohol together were above those with either alone and close to the sum of their separate excesses (at 0.05 g/100 mL: 1.81 with both, 1.66 with alcohol alone, 1.16 with THC alone, against drivers with neither), and THC's added effect shrank as alcohol rose (THC by blood alcohol interaction odds ratio 0.987 per 0.01 g/100 mL, 0.981 to 0.994). Read for this library from the accepted manuscript; a different design and outcome from this simulator study, and not a repeat of it.

Rogeberg and Elvik (Addiction): re-analysis of the meta-analyses that this paper's Discussion recalls as showing doubled crash risk. After re-extracting counts and using adjusted estimates, the pooled odds ratio for 28 estimates from 21 studies was 1.36 (1.15 to 1.61; random effects) or 1.22 (1.10 to 1.36; small-study-adjusted); estimates from studies that controlled for alcohol were lower (1.11 and 1.18) than those that did not (1.79 and 1.69). Read for this library.

replication.where_it_stands: As the paper itself describes them, the few simulator and on-road studies of the combination disagree: this study and Lenné 2010 found no interaction on lane position, while Ronen 2010 and the on-road work of Robbe and Ramaekers found effects with the combination that neither drug showed alone. This study's no-interaction finding rests on a stepwise model with no estimate for the interaction, so its combined values are sums by construction. A large real-world analysis read for this library (Dubois et al., 2015) found the combination close to the sum of the single-drug excesses, with THC adding little to alcohol at 0.05 to 0.08 g/100 mL, but that is a different outcome (a recorded unsafe driver action in fatal crashes) and design. The 'about doubled' crash risk that this paper's Discussion recalls was revised downwards in a 2016 re-analysis (Rogeberg and Elvik). No on-road study of the combination was read.

funding.funder: US Office of National Drug Control Policy; Intramural Research Program, National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (Role of Funding Source).
funding.declared_conflicts: The vaporizer and oral-fluid collection devices and supplies (Storz and Bickel; Immunalysis) were provided by their manufacturers through Materials Transfer Agreements; no commercial entity played a role in design, conduct, analysis, writing or the decision to publish; the authors declare no personal conflicts of interest (Conflicts of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The affiliation list was collapsed on the page and was not extracted. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered, adequately powered randomized factorial crossover study of several THC and alcohol levels, analysed with the interaction estimated and reported with its interval (and with the person and the drive, not the single event, as the unit of analysis), in an on-road or high-fidelity simulator test that also includes regular cannabis smokers and women, with the achieved concentrations during the drive measured or tightly bracketed, and with outcomes tied to crash-relevant events such as lane departures and braking.

domains.note: Order is stated as randomized, but sequence generation, concealment and the sequences used are not described. Within-person contrasts remove between-person confounding.

Sessions at least 1 week apart, but no period effect is modelled, scenario assignment to sessions is not described, and baseline blood THC was above zero in some sessions (up to 6.3 µg/L, Table 6), consistent with use between sessions or carryover.

Double-blinding is stated only in the Discussion and Conclusion; how it was kept or checked is not described, and the effects of cannabis and of alcohol at these levels are perceptible. Inhalation was ad libitum, so achieved THC differed from assigned dose and overlapped between doses; analysis by achieved concentration is not protected by the randomization.
18 of 19 analysed and no dropouts reported; the one exclusion was made from the driving data themselves and is counted under selection of the reported result.

SDLP and the other measures are automated simulator records. During-drive THC and alcohol were modelled from samples before and after the drive, which adds uncertainty about the exposure but is not a bias in the outcome.

No sample-size calculation or analysis plan in the paper and the registry record was not read. The headline model is a data-driven stepwise selection on modelled concentrations, used after the by-condition mixed models were not significant; hundreds of variables were monitored and only the lateral-control subset is reported; one extreme participant was excluded after the data were seen; no correction across six models.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 is applied as for a crossover trial. The randomized, placebo-controlled within-person contrasts are protected against confounding, but the paper's headline estimates are regressions on achieved, partly self-titrated concentrations chosen by a stepwise procedure, with event-level standard errors that treat repeated events as independent. Four of six domains raise some concerns; none is judged high because the exposure was administered under control, the outcome is automated and the dropout is minimal. The source may be cited for the direction of the associations between during-drive THC or breath alcohol and lane weave in 18 healthy occasional cannabis smokers in a simulator, and for the lane-departure and lateral-acceleration results for alcohol. It may not be cited for synergy or for the absence of synergy, for the THC and alcohol equivalences as if they had intervals, for real-road crash risk, or for effects in regular cannabis smokers.

key_findings.finding: 19 healthy adults drove (13 men, 6 women; ages 21 to 37, mean 26.1, SD 4.1; 74% White). Participant 12, a woman, was excluded from all driving analyses because her data were extreme in almost every measure and condition, including placebo with placebo, with markedly erratic driving on video, leaving 18 analysed (13 men and 5 women by the editors' count from Table 1; mean age 26.3, SD 4.2).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (row 12 and the N = 18 summary rows)
key_findings.note: The abstract calls the 18 completers; all 19 completed the sessions.

key_findings.finding: Six conditions (placebo, 2.9% or 6.7% THC vaporized cannabis, each with placebo or alcohol) in randomized order, at least 1 week apart. Alcohol drunk over 10 minutes, aimed at an approximate peak breath alcohol of 0.065%, then 500 mg of cannabis inhaled over 10 minutes; a 45-minute night drive (urban, interstate, rural segments) began 0.5 to 1.3 hours after the start of cannabis dosing; three scenario variants limited practice effects.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.2 Study Design/Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.4 Drives, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: During-drive blood THC was modelled by individual power-curve regression from samples at 0.17, 0.42, 1.4 and 2.3 hours, and breath alcohol by linear interpolation. Driving data were analysed by event with SAS GLM Select (stepwise, Schwarz information criterion; candidate terms blood THC, breath alcohol, their product, speed limit, inverse curvature, subject; effect hierarchy not enforced). Quadratic terms for THC and alcohol were added to test for a ceiling effect and neither was selected.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.6 Data Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › 3.2 Driving, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Achieved blood THC overlapped between the two active doses: 6 participants had a higher peak after the low than the high dose and 4 had peaks within 20% of each other despite a two-fold dose difference. The authors therefore analysed by concentration and call analysis by dose group not scientifically meaningful. They infer self-titration of inhalation and, from a companion paper (not read), say 52.6% of participants showed evidence of it.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Figure 3 (image; values not extracted); Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: SDLP model: blood THC b = 0.26 cm per µg/L (SE 0.07, t = 3.6, p = 0.0004); breath alcohol b = 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L (SE 0.15, t = 2.9, p = 0.0037); no THC by alcohol term selected; speed limit 0.50 (SE 0.03) and inverse curvature 464 (SE 49); model df 21, F 28.24, error df 1,916. Increases of 0.8% per µg/L THC and 1.3% per 0.01 g/210 L breath alcohol relative to the drug-free median SDLP.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 1st paragraph; Table 2, SDLP block
key_findings.note: Table 2 does not state the unit of the alcohol estimate; 0.42 is per 0.01 g/210 L as given in the text and Table 3.

key_findings.finding: Model predictions at 55 mph on a straight road (Table 3): drug-free median SDLP 31.4 cm (between-person range 24.7 to 44.8). THC 1, 2, 5, 7, 10 and 20 µg/L: +0.26, +0.52, +1.3, +1.8, +2.6, +5.2 cm (0.8%, 1.6%, 4.1%, 5.8%, 8.2%, 16%). Breath alcohol 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L: +0.42, +0.84, +2.1, +3.4, +4.2 cm (1.3%, 2.7%, 6.7%, 11%, 13%). THC 2 µg/L with alcohol 0.05: +2.6 cm (8.4%); THC 5 µg/L with alcohol 0.05: +3.4 cm (11%), the same as alcohol 0.08 alone (+3.4 cm, 11%).
key_findings.note: The combined rows equal the sum of the single effects because the selected model has no interaction term; they are model outputs, not observed values.

key_findings.finding: Stated equivalences: breath alcohol of 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L, the most common legal limits, gave lane weave like blood THC of 8.2 and 13.1 µg/L; THC of 1 and 2 µg/L gave increases like 0.01 g/210 L; at 5 and 10 µg/L SDLP rose 4.1% and 8.2%, against 6.7% for alcohol 0.05 and 11% for alcohol 0.08.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › 3.2 Driving, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend (image; values not extracted)
key_findings.note: No intervals are given for the equivalences.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol, not THC, increased the less sensitive measures: lane departures per minute (b = 0.030, SE 0.009, t = 2.8, p = 0.0055) and maximum lateral acceleration in events without sharp turns (b = 0.0023 m/s², SE 0.0007, t = 3.5, p = 0.0005); at 0.05 g/210 L these rose 35% (0.13 per minute) and 9.5% (0.11 m/s²), at 0.08 g/210 L 55% and 15%. THC was not selected in either model; neither drug affected steering-angle variability or acceleration in sharp events.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 (lane departures, steering angle and acceleration blocks); Table 3

key_findings.finding: Mean SDLP by administered condition, 18 drivers each (Table 5, second block): placebo with placebo 28.8 cm (SD 17.8); alcohol alone 32.3 (+3.5 cm, +12%); low THC alone 31.3 (+9%); high THC alone 31.2 (+8%); low THC with alcohol 34.2 (+19%); high THC with alcohol 32.2 (+12%). Lane departures per minute: 0.52 placebo; 0.74 alcohol alone; 0.73 low THC with alcohol; 0.80 high THC with alcohol. No statistical test or interval is given for these means.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Table 5, administered dose conditions
key_findings.note: The Table 5 note says analysis of variance could not be conducted by dose condition because of unbalanced cells from self-titration, but these cells are balanced (18 each); the by-dose comparison could have been tested.

key_findings.finding: By achieved peak THC group (median split at 8.6 µg/L; Table 5, first block), mean SDLP: placebo with placebo 28.8 cm (N = 18); no alcohol, below-median THC 32.3 (N = 11, +12%) and above-median 29.8 (N = 12, +3%); with alcohol, placebo THC 32.3 (N = 18, +12%), below-median 34.6 (N = 18, +20%), above-median 32.2 (N = 16, +12%). Repeated-measures linear mixed model by group, SDLP: THC group p = 0.28, alcohol p = 0.067, THC by alcohol p = 0.24; lane departures per minute p = 0.45, 0.13, 0.12; acceleration p = 0.25, 0.092, 0.49. The authors say this analysis has low power and uncertain interpretation.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Table 4; Table 5, achieved concentration conditions
key_findings.note: See reporting issue 1 on duplicated SDLP values in this table.

key_findings.finding: Mean (SD) blood THC in all 19 participants, in µg/L, with 2.9% and 6.7% cannabis without alcohol and with alcohol: 0.17 hours 35.9 (16.7), 56.2 (36.4), 40.5 (18.2), 75.0 (48.1); 0.42 hours 10.0 (4.5), 16.8 (10.9), 10.4 (3.4), 19.0 (11.9); 1.4 hours 3.9 (2.3), 5.7 (3.9), 3.6 (1.4), 6.8 (4.6); 2.3 hours 2.2 (1.8), 3.2 (2.6), 1.8 (1.1), 3.2 (2.5). Pre-dose baseline median 0, up to 6.3. Between-person variability was larger for oral fluid THC than for blood at every time point (coefficients of variation 125% to 207% against 45% to 65% at the first post-dose sample; the Discussion calls it 2- to 5-fold).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Pre- and Post-drive Blood and OF THC Concentrations, 1st paragraph; Table 6; Discussion, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: Mean blood THC at the first sample was higher with alcohol than without (75.0 against 56.2 at 6.7%; 40.5 against 35.9 at 2.9%); the paper does not test this.

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: participants know driving is observed and may drive more carefully or may want to show cannabis does not affect driving; only occasional cannabis smokers were studied, and frequent smokers show tolerance to some effects; the stepwise procedure was used to describe the data without assuming which terms matter; and they do not regard use of a simulator rather than a road as a significant limitation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.1 Strengths and limitations, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: US Office of National Drug Control Policy, NIDA Intramural Research Program and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Devices and supplies supplied by manufacturers under Materials Transfer Agreements; no personal conflicts declared. Registered as NCT01620177.
key_findings.locator: Role of Funding Source; Conflicts of Interest; Clinical Trial Registration (end matter)

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 5 (first block) the row for below-median THC with placebo alcohol (N = 11) prints exactly the same SDLP values as the row for placebo THC with alcohol (N = 18): mean 32.3 cm, SD 21.7, difference 3.5 cm, 12%. The second block gives 32.3 cm with SD 19.3 for placebo THC with alcohol, so the same condition has two different SDs (21.7 and 19.3). The lane-departure and acceleration columns of the two rows differ.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of these SDLP entries is a transcription error. The by-group means cannot be relied on to judge whether lane weave rises with achieved THC; the claim uses them only descriptively and cites the administered-dose block.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract refers to 18 completers, but all 19 participants completed the sessions; one was excluded from every driving analysis after review of the driving data and videos. No exclusion rule set in advance and no analysis that keeps participant 12 are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: A post hoc, outcome-informed exclusion; as her data were extreme in the placebo condition too, a large effect on the drug contrasts is unlikely, but this cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that at or above 8.2 µg/L THC the study met the lowest criterion of impairment, about 2.4 cm (the SDLP increase at 0.05 blood alcohol in a cited report). By the paper's own coefficients 8.2 µg/L gives about 2.1 cm (Table 3: 7 µg/L 1.8 cm, 10 µg/L 2.6 cm), so the 2.4 cm criterion is reached at about 9 µg/L; 2.1 cm is the study's own 0.05 g/210 L equivalent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement mixes the external 2.4 cm benchmark with the study's own 2.1 cm equivalent; the difference is small but the abstract's THC thresholds are point estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The THC and alcohol equivalences (8.2 and 13.1 µg/L for 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L) are ratios of two slopes (0.26, SE 0.07; 0.42, SE 0.15) given without intervals. Editors' calculation by the delta method, covariance ignored: about 8 µg/L with an approximate 95% interval of about 1 to 15 µg/L for the 0.05 equivalent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The equivalences are far less precise than the abstract's wording suggests; they cannot support a precise concentration limit.

reporting_issues.issue: The range of during-drive THC and breath alcohol values analysed is not reported. The alcohol dose was aimed at a peak of about 0.065%, yet Table 3 predicts lane weave at 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L, and the abstract compares THC with 0.08.
reporting_issues.consequence: The predictions at 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L (and the 13.1 µg/L equivalence) may lie beyond the data, which would make them extrapolations; the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: Error degrees of freedom in the models are 1,916 (SDLP), 427 and 1,936 (steering angle), 840 (lane departures) and 2,026 and 304 (acceleration), for data from 18 drivers in 108 drives (18 drivers by 6 conditions). For SDLP that is about 18 events per drive treated as independent observations, with a subject term only for each person's average.
reporting_issues.consequence: Standard errors and p-values for THC and alcohol are probably too small (editors' inference; the paper does not describe correction for repeated events), so the intervals calculated from them are likely too narrow.

reporting_issues.issue: The finding of additive, not synergistic, effects is drawn from the absence of a THC by alcohol term in a stepwise model selected by an information criterion. No estimate or interval for the interaction is given. Table 3's combined rows are sums by construction.
reporting_issues.consequence: Additivity here is the model's structure, not a measured result; the paper cannot be cited as showing that the combination is no worse than the sum.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5's note says analysis of variance could not be conducted by dose condition, but the administered-dose cells are balanced (18 each) and the by-dose block was reported only as descriptive means.
reporting_issues.consequence: Contrasts by administered dose were not tested; the descriptive means show no ordering between low and high THC (+9% and +8% alone; +19% and +12% with alcohol).

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say all participants reported driving at least once a week, but participant 2 gave no response for driving frequency or years of driving (Table 1, footnote c). Table 1 also gives 120 days since last cannabis use for participant 13 (analysed), which is outside the inclusion window of use at least once in the past 3 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both are self-reports and the eligibility checks cannot be audited from the paper.

The three supplementary files (one docx, two pdf) were not read.
